newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen backs Euro nationalist link-up.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen backs Euro nationalist link-up.

text.p: Shrugging off a mass protest against his National Front party, France's Jean-Marie Le Pen urged European far-rightists on Sunday to join forces and launched work on a battle plan for the 1998 elections.

"We propose in coming days a form of...political cooperation between our countries. Why not call this 'Euro-Nat' -- a grouping of the Europe of nationalists, of the Europe of nationals," Le Pen told a party congress in Strasbourg.

Le Pen spoke after several other European rightists including Ricardo Saenz de Ynestrillas, president of Spain's Alianza Unidad Nacional, Frank Vanhecke, president of Belgium's Vlaams Blok, and former German European Parliament deputy Hans-Gunter Schodruch.
"Mr Le Pen is in the vanguard of the nationalist movement," Saenz de Ynestrillas told cheering delegates on the second day of the Front's three-day congress.
A day earlier, an estimated 40,000 anti-Front protesters marched through the streets of the eastern French city.

The congress was convened to elect party leaders and plot strategy for gaining a foothold in parliament in March 1998 general elections. The Front now has no seats in parliament despite Le Pen's 15 percent showing in a 1995 presidential poll.

Le Pen told reporters he believed the Front would win "10 or 20 seats" in 1998 and could win more if there were "explosive events" such as a mass exodus to France of Algerians fleeing civil strife between the authorities and Moslem rebels.

In anticipation of victory, Le Pen set up working groups to draft a legislative programme including a plan to repatriate immigrants and a proposed constitutional amendment to give preference in education, jobs and social benefits to "native-born" French people.

March organisers boasted that the protest, which went off peacefully and was believed to be the largest ever assembled against Le Pen, marked a turning point in their campaign to curb the Front's influence in French politics.
But its impact was marred by evening clashes between police and young people after the march had ended.

Three police officers were slightly hurt, 21 shop windows shattered and 38 people taken into custody after the clashes, including five or six Germans and a Dutchman, police said. Most of the 38 were still behind bars on Sunday, they said.
In one violent clash, police fired teargas at stonethrowers trying to reach the Strasbourg conference centre, where the 2,200 Front delegates met under extremely tight security.
In a second confrontation, police used teargas and a water cannon as demonstrators went on a rampage at a rock concert in the city centre.
Strasbourg's Socialist mayor, Catherine Trautmann, condemned the violence and cancelled a second concert set for Sunday night.
Le Pen, in the second of three major speeches he was to deliver during the three-day congress, accused the protesters of "an organised attack on democracy and on the republic".

He said that some 180,000 Strasbourg voters had backed him in 1995 presidential elections, far more than had marched, and suggested sending a bill for the damage to "Cathy the Red" -- a reference to Trautmann, who had led the demonstration.
Delegates then re-elected Le Pen president by acclamation.
The 68-year-old leader was unopposed and has refused to publicly discuss the question of a successor.

But his deputies Bruno Gollnisch and Bruno Megret exposed their ambitions in open wrangling for the upper hand in elections to the party's key central committee. Megret later boasted to reporters that he had won more votes than his rival.

Le Pen, who has denied he is racist or anti-Semitic, said his voters were excluded from the French mainstream and compared them to "a caste of less-than-citizens, pariahs who remind us of plague victims during the Middle Ages or the Jews of Nazi Germany".
